## Guided Tutorial 10.1: Joining the Variance to Its Work Orders and Products

**Context and objective.** The WorkOrderClose table records each variance but not the product that produced it. In this tutorial, you will join the closes to their work orders and items, test that every close finds its match, and summarize the variance by item group and year. You will check the total against the ledger, keep the items that carry the most variance with HAVING, and list every manufactured item with a left join, including the items with no closes.

**Prerequisites.** Complete Chapter 9, and open CharlesRiver_Work.sqlite in DB Browser for SQLite on the **Execute SQL** tab. Start a new script for the chapter with the header comment below, with your own name and the date, and click **Save SQL file** to save it as `Chapter10.sql` beside your working copy. As in Chapter 9, type each query of the chapter's tutorials at the end of the script, under its comment, and run it by selecting it.

```sql
/* Chapter 10: manufacturing variance, joined and summarized
   Database: CharlesRiver_Work.sqlite (a copy of CharlesRiver.sqlite)
   Prepared by: your name, date
   Checks: listed at the end of Tutorial 10.3 */
```

**Step-by-step instructions.**

**Step 1. Join the closes to their work orders, and test the join.** Each close carries the WorkOrderID of the work order it closes, and an inner join that finds every match returns one row for each close.

a. Type and run the query below.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 10.1: the closes joined to their work orders
   SELECT woc.WorkOrderCloseID, woc.CloseDate, wo.WorkOrderNumber,
       wo.ItemID, woc.TotalVarianceAmount
   FROM WorkOrderClose AS woc
       INNER JOIN WorkOrder AS wo ON wo.WorkOrderID = woc.WorkOrderID;
   ```

b. Read the number of rows in the message pane.
c. Type and run the query below, and compare the two numbers.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 10.1: the number of closes, to test the join
   SELECT COUNT(*) AS Closes
   FROM WorkOrderClose;
   ```

The join returns exactly as many rows as the WorkOrderClose table holds, many thousands. Every close therefore matches one work order, and none has been dropped by the inner join.

**Step 2. Add the items.** The work order's ItemID leads to the Item table.

a. Type and run the query below, which adds a second join and the item's columns.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 10.1: the closes with their items
   SELECT woc.WorkOrderCloseID, woc.CloseDate, i.ItemCode,
       i.ItemName, i.ItemGroup, woc.TotalVarianceAmount
   FROM WorkOrderClose AS woc
       INNER JOIN WorkOrder AS wo ON wo.WorkOrderID = woc.WorkOrderID
       INNER JOIN Item AS i ON i.ItemID = wo.ItemID;
   ```

b. Confirm that the number of rows is the same as in Step 1.

Each close now carries the code, name, and group of the item its work order made. The row count is unchanged, so every work order matches an item.

**Step 3. Total the variance of fiscal 2026 by item group, and check it against the ledger.** A summary is only useful if it agrees with the books.

a. Type and run the query below.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 10.1: the variance of fiscal 2026 by item group
   SELECT i.ItemGroup, COUNT(*) AS Closes,
       ROUND(SUM(woc.TotalVarianceAmount), 2) AS TotalVariance
   FROM WorkOrderClose AS woc
       INNER JOIN WorkOrder AS wo ON wo.WorkOrderID = woc.WorkOrderID
       INNER JOIN Item AS i ON i.ItemID = wo.ItemID
   WHERE woc.CloseDate BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-12-31'
   GROUP BY i.ItemGroup
   ORDER BY TotalVariance DESC;
   ```

b. Type and run the query below, which totals the variance postings of fiscal 2026 in the ledger that Tutorial 9.2 isolated.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 10.1: the same variance in the ledger
   SELECT ROUND(SUM(gl.Debit) - SUM(gl.Credit), 2) AS LedgerVariance
   FROM GLEntry AS gl
   WHERE gl.AccountID = 93 AND gl.FiscalYear = 2026
       AND gl.SourceDocumentType = 'WorkOrderClose';
   ```

c. Add up the TotalVariance column of item a, and compare it with the ledger total.

Three item groups carry the variance: Furniture, Lighting, and Textiles, the groups whose items Charles River makes in quantity. Furniture holds more than two-thirds of it. The three groups add up to the ledger total to the cent, so the work order records and the ledger tell the same story.

**Step 4. Compare the three years.** The year of a close is the first four characters of its CloseDate, and GROUP BY can use the alias CloseYear that the SELECT list gives it.

a. Type and run the query below.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 10.1: the variance by item group and year
   SELECT i.ItemGroup, SUBSTR(woc.CloseDate, 1, 4) AS CloseYear,
       COUNT(*) AS Closes,
       ROUND(SUM(woc.TotalVarianceAmount), 2) AS TotalVariance,
       ROUND(SUM(woc.OverheadVarianceAmount), 2) AS OverheadVariance
   FROM WorkOrderClose AS woc
       INNER JOIN WorkOrder AS wo ON wo.WorkOrderID = woc.WorkOrderID
       INNER JOIN Item AS i ON i.ItemID = wo.ItemID
   GROUP BY i.ItemGroup, CloseYear
   ORDER BY i.ItemGroup, CloseYear;
   ```

b. For each item group, compare the three years of TotalVariance and of Closes.

The result, shown in @fig-10-03, holds one row for each group and year. Furniture's variance rose in each year, to nearly twice its fiscal 2024 level, and Lighting's rose too, while Textiles rose and then fell back in fiscal 2026. In every group, the number of closes fell over the same period, so a larger variance was spread over fewer work orders. The overhead part moves with the total in each group.

![The Manufacturing Variance by Item Group and Year.](/visuals/svg/fig-10-03-variance-by-group-year.svg){#fig-10-03 fig-alt="A mock of the Execute SQL tab. The editor, on the tab Chapter10.sql, is scrolled to a comment and a query that joins WorkOrderClose to WorkOrder and Item and groups the closes by item group and close year, with the number of closes, the total variance, and the overhead variance. The result holds nine rows, three years each for Furniture, Lighting, and Textiles. The Furniture rows, whose total variance rises in each year while the number of closes falls, are outlined."}

**Step 5. Keep the items that carry the most variance.** WHERE keeps the closes of fiscal 2026, and HAVING then keeps the items whose total passes a threshold. Group by the item's key, and include its code and name so that the result is readable.

a. Type and run the query below.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 10.1: items with more than $50,000 of variance in 2026
   SELECT i.ItemID, i.ItemCode, i.ItemName, COUNT(*) AS Closes,
       ROUND(SUM(woc.TotalVarianceAmount), 2) AS TotalVariance
   FROM WorkOrderClose AS woc
       INNER JOIN WorkOrder AS wo ON wo.WorkOrderID = woc.WorkOrderID
       INNER JOIN Item AS i ON i.ItemID = wo.ItemID
   WHERE woc.CloseDate BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-12-31'
   GROUP BY i.ItemID, i.ItemCode, i.ItemName
   HAVING SUM(woc.TotalVarianceAmount) > 50000
   ORDER BY TotalVariance DESC;
   ```

b. Read the items and their totals, and note the item groups they come from.
c. Change 50000 to 30000, run the query again, and read the number of rows.
d. Change the threshold back to 50000.

Only a handful of items pass the threshold of item a, a mix of dining tables, sideboards, and a throw blanket, each with a few dozen closes. At the lower threshold, several times as many pass. No single item stands out, and the largest carries only a small share of the year's variance. The variance is spread across most of the items Charles River makes, which points to a cause that affects production as a whole rather than one product.

**Step 6. List every manufactured item, including those with no closes.** A complete list starts from the table that holds the whole population, the items, and left joins the others to it.

a. Type and run the query below.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 10.1: every manufactured item with its closes of 2026
   SELECT i.ItemCode, i.ItemName, i.LifecycleStatus,
       COUNT(woc.WorkOrderCloseID) AS Closes2026
   FROM Item AS i
       LEFT JOIN WorkOrder AS wo ON wo.ItemID = i.ItemID
       LEFT JOIN WorkOrderClose AS woc ON woc.WorkOrderID = wo.WorkOrderID
           AND woc.CloseDate BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-12-31'
   WHERE i.SupplyMode = 'Manufactured'
   GROUP BY i.ItemID, i.ItemCode, i.ItemName, i.LifecycleStatus
   ORDER BY Closes2026, i.ItemCode;
   ```

b. Read the number of rows and the first rows of the result.
c. Move the date condition from the ON clause to the WHERE clause, by deleting it from the second join and adding `AND woc.CloseDate BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-12-31'` to the WHERE clause, and run the query again.
d. Compare the number of rows with item b, and then move the condition back into the ON clause.

The query of item a returns one row for every manufactured item, and the first rows show a handful with no closes at all, each counted as zero by `COUNT(woc.WorkOrderCloseID)`. They are discontinued items. With the date condition in WHERE, those items disappear, because their close columns are NULL and a NULL CloseDate is not in any range. The left join has become an inner join, the trap of the section on left joins.

**Checkpoint.** Check that:

- the joins in Steps 1 and 2 return as many rows as the WorkOrderClose table holds;
- the variance of fiscal 2026 by item group adds up to the ledger total of Step 3;
- Furniture carries most of the variance, and its variance rose in each year while its number of closes fell;
- HAVING keeps only a handful of items above $50,000, spread across several product types;
- the complete list of Step 6 keeps the items with no closes only while the date condition is in the ON clause;
- Chapter10.sql holds the header and the queries of this tutorial, each under a comment.

The variance is not a product problem. It rises in the groups the plant makes most, while the number of work orders falls, and that pattern turns the question toward the cost of production itself.
